subject: no-code-automation
question: Will every applicant receive their joining link?

artifact.workflow:
Form field 'Email' is a plain text box (no validation).
Workflow: New submission -> send confirmation email with the event joining link to {{email}}.
AI: "Every applicant receives their joining link."

ai_claim: Yes. The workflow emails the address each applicant entered, so everyone receives the link.

ai_solution.text: Each applicant enters an email address.
The workflow sends to that address.
Email delivery reaches the applicant.
So everyone receives the link.

failure.explanation: A plain text box accepts typos ('asha@gmial.com', 'asha@gmail', spaces), so some emails bounce or go to strangers, and those applicants never get the link - silently. Use an email-type field with validation, a confirmation field or double opt-in, and monitor bounces with a follow-up path.
failure.why_convincing: Most people type their email correctly.

canonical_solution: No: typos and invalid addresses mean some applicants never receive the link. Validate emails and handle bounces.

valid_evidence.summary: Validate user input at the source and monitor delivery failures.

counterexamples: An applicant with a typo never gets the link.

hints.text: Think about what people type by mistake.
Step 3 assumes every address works.
Validate inputs and monitor bounces.
Look at bounce reports.
Step 3 is wrong: invalid addresses bounce. Validate and follow up.

repair: Use an email field with validation, and route bounces to a follow-up process.
debrief: Garbage in the form becomes silent failure in the workflow. Validate at the source.

subject: no-code-automation
subtopic: A response sheet anyone can edit
question: Is 'anyone with the link can edit' acceptable for this sheet?

artifact.workflow:
Job-application form responses (name, phone, address, CV link) go to a Google Sheet.
Sharing: 'Anyone with the link can edit' so the hiring panel can open it easily.
AI: "Only people we send the link to will see it, so this is fine."

ai_claim: Yes. The link is only shared with the hiring panel, so only they can access the sheet.

ai_solution.text: The link is shared with the panel.
Others do not have the link.
Without the link, nobody can open it.
So only the panel has access.

failure.misconception: Protecting personal data with a shareable link
failure.explanation: Links are forwarded, pasted into chats and calendars, and saved in browser history; anyone who obtains it can read and edit applicants' personal data - with no record of who did. Edit access also lets anyone alter or delete responses. Share with named accounts only (viewers where possible), restrict to the organisation, and review access.

canonical_solution: No: anyone with the link can view and edit applicants' personal data. Share with named people only.

valid_evidence.summary: A panel member pastes the link into a group chat with external recruiters, who can now edit the sheet.
Personal data should be shared with named, authenticated users on a least-privilege basis.

counterexamples: A forwarded link exposes every applicant's address and phone.

hints.text: Ask how links spread.
Step 2 assumes the link stays private.
Link sharing is not access control.
Consider a forwarded link.
Step 2 is wrong: links leak. Restrict to named users.

repair: Restrict sharing to named accounts (view-only for most), within the organisation.
debrief: Convenient sharing settings are a common source of personal-data leaks in no-code setups.

subject: no-code-automation
question: Is the AI right?

artifact.workflow:
The form platform assigns each submission a unique Submission ID.
Workflow: New submission -> search the sheet for this Submission ID -> if not found, add a row; if found, skip.
AI: "Re-sent or replayed webhook events won't create duplicate rows."

ai_claim: Yes. Each submission has one unique ID, and the workflow adds a row only if that ID is not already in the sheet, so replays of the same submission are skipped.

ai_solution.text: Each submission has a unique ID.
The workflow checks the sheet for that ID.
Replays carry the same ID and are found.
So duplicates are skipped.

canonical_solution: Correct. Checking for a unique ID before inserting makes the workflow idempotent against duplicate deliveries (two truly simultaneous deliveries could still race, which is rare).

valid_evidence.summary: Replaying submission S-2291 twice leaves one row for S-2291.

hints.text: Follow a replayed event.
Step 3 relies on the ID being the same.
Unique keys make inserts idempotent.
Replay one submission.
This solution is correct. Duplicates are skipped. The right judgment was to approve it.

debrief: Every integration that can deliver twice should check a unique key before creating records.

subject: no-code-automation
subtopic: Mail merge with a test send
question: Is the AI right that this is a sound process for a bulk personalised email?

artifact.workflow:
Mail merge from a sheet (columns: first_name, course, start_date) to 480 students.
Before sending, the workflow sends one test email to the organiser using the first row, checks placeholders render correctly, and then sends the rest in batches of 50.

ai_claim: Yes. The test send catches broken placeholders and formatting before 480 people see them, and batching reduces the risk of hitting sending limits or spreading a mistake.

ai_solution.text: A test email uses real data from the first row.
The organiser checks every placeholder.
Only then does the bulk send start.
Batches limit the damage if something goes wrong.

canonical_solution: Correct. Test-first and batched sending are standard safeguards for mail merges.

valid_evidence.summary: The test email shows 'Hi {{firstname}}' unrendered, revealing a column-name mismatch before any student receives it.

hints.text: Ask what could go wrong in a mail merge.
Step 2 catches placeholder errors.
Test with real data before bulk actions.
Consider a misnamed column.
This solution is correct. The process catches errors early. The right judgment was to approve it.

debrief: Bulk actions multiply mistakes. A single realistic test send is the cheapest safeguard.

subject: no-code-automation
question: Will all 1,200 applicants receive the email today?

artifact.workflow:
Workflow sends the admit letter to 1,200 applicants through a connected Gmail account at 10:00 today.
Which kind of Gmail account is connected (a free consumer account or a Google Workspace account), and its sending history today, are not recorded.

ai_claim: Yes. The workflow sends to all 1,200 applicants, so everyone receives it today.

ai_solution.text: The list has 1,200 applicants.
The workflow sends one email to each.
Gmail delivers each email.
So everyone receives it today.

missing_information: The connected account's sending limits. Gmail enforces daily sending limits - roughly 500 recipients per day for a free account and around 2,000 messages per day for a Google Workspace account - and emails already sent today count too. Which account type is connected is not recorded.
resolving_scenarios: A Google Workspace account with little prior sending today: all 1,200 emails can be sent.
A free consumer Gmail account: sending stops after about 500 recipients, and the remaining ~700 fail until the limit resets.
canonical_solution: It depends on the account type and today's usage, which are unknown. Step 3 assumes no sending limits.

valid_evidence.summary: On a free Gmail account, about 700 of the 1,200 sends would fail with a sending-limit error.

counterexamples: Sending halts partway through on a consumer account.

hints.text: Ask what limits the sending account has.
Step 3 assumes unlimited sending.
Email providers enforce daily sending limits by account type.
Compare 1,200 with a 500-per-day limit.
Step 3 assumes no limits. Workspace can send all; a free account cannot. It cannot be decided.

repair: Check the account's limits; use a transactional email service for bulk sends.
debrief: Bulk sending through a personal mailbox hits limits and deliverability problems. Use a service built for it.
